# The prompt queue — the contract `ai.js` is built against

This is the wire contract for prompts a person types while a reply is still
running. All three parts have shipped: the UI (PRD 5.4), the durable half
(PRD 5.3), and the wire between them (PRD 7.6). **This document was the
specification 5.3 had to satisfy, and it is now the record of what all three
agreed to.** §10 says what 7.6 built, which of §9's questions the server had
already answered by the time it started, and the one it had to answer itself.

Two things below are no longer true as written, and are marked where they
appear rather than edited away, because being able to see what was believed
before a thing was built is most of this file's value: §7's *"the queue is
lost on a reload"* now holds only for a chat with no durable backing, and §9's
questions are all closed.

It sits beside `ai-question-frame.md` for the same reason that one does: it is
an internal contract between two halves of one feature, not public SDK
documentation, and it belongs next to the file that consumes it. Section
references of the form §4.5 without a document name are to the question-frame
contract.

Everything below is binding on the server unless it says otherwise.

## The short version

* **A queued prompt is durable, and 5.3 pays a model and a migration for it.**
  Open question 12 is settled in §1.
* **The server stores and orders the queue. It never runs it.** A live client
  is the only thing that starts a turn, because a server that starts one
  breaks the reconcile in every `ai.js` on the CDN today (§1.2).
* **A queue row hangs off `Chat`, never off `Message`** (§2.1). This is the
  single line that makes "survives an interrupt" structural instead of a
  promise.
* **Nothing may be queued, and nothing may RUN BY ITSELF, while a reply in
  that chat is `awaiting_input`** (§4). The server enforces it; the client's
  gate is read off the trail, not off `generating` (§4.2).
* **A person's own press is never refused for a reason they cannot see or
  undo** (§4.4). This is the rule the first cut of 5.4 broke, and it is worth
  as much as the one above it.
* **An interrupt holds the queue: it never drains it and never clears it, and
  the thing doing the interrupting must SAY SO before the socket ends** (§5).
  Written before 5.5 exists, so 5.5 cannot decide it by accident.
* **5.4 ships today against every server alive, and makes zero new requests**
  (§7). The answer to "useful or harmless with no server support" is
  **useful**, with the bound stated on the strip itself and not only here.

---

## 0. What was driven, and what it changed

Every claim below marked *(driven)* was reproduced against the real runtime
through `tests/ai/harness.mjs`, not read off the source.

| Believed | Driven | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a mid-stream prompt is "dropped" at Enter | Enter fires nothing and clears nothing; the words sit in the box and a later press sends them. They die **later**, invisibly, when a re-render rebuilds the composer | the harm is a *silent* rebuild, not a refusal — so the fix needs a draft that survives a render as much as it needs a queue (§6.3) |
| the composer is locked for the whole of a paused turn (§4.5, shipped) | after the fifteen-minute tail limit frees `S.sending`, the send button is correctly `disabled` and **Enter posts a second turn and starts a second reply stream** | a live defect in shipped 5.2, fixed by reading `waitingOnYou()` and not `S.sending` (§6.1) |
| `S.sending` gates the chat you are in | it is module-global: a reply streaming in chat A silently swallows everything typed in chat B, and on `/new` fires no request at all | the queue is per chat but the *slot* is global, which decides the drain rule (§6.2) |
| a wider "the server says it is generating" lock protects an unseeable pause | it **wedges the chat permanently**: `generating` is written once by the reconcile and never re-read, so one documented approval pause left the composer refusing every message for the rest of the page session, with no button, no error and a note promising a send that could never happen | the lock came out of the composer entirely, the queue's gate moved to the trail, and §4.4 exists (§6.1) |
| an approval pause has no card, so the gate has to stand in for one | it has no card **because of a rendering defect**, not because one is impossible: `approvalPromptNode` was reached only from `renderAiMessage`, which builds a reply node once | the approval is a sync site now, exactly like the question box, and the pause is on the screen with the controls that end it (§3.3) |
| putting a queued row back in the box is a free edit | it is `input.innerText = text` — a **replace**. Driven: an unsent follow-up, and a half-typed answer, both destroyed by one click with no undo and nothing stashed | the take-back is a swap, and it is refused outright while a question is pending (§4.3) |
| the optimistic echo consoles somebody whose send failed | the echo keeps a `local-` id the server has never seen, nothing marks it failed, there is no retry, and one refetch erases it | a POST that never landed puts the words back in the queue and takes the phantom off the thread (§6.4) |
| "an interrupt never runs the queue" is already implemented | true for a **rejected read**, false for a **clean close** — which is what a stop that kills the worker produces, and what the only interrupt this surface already has (Decline) produces | `stopStream` exists, `commitStream` reads it, and 5.5 is bound to call it (§5) |

## 1. Open question 12, settled: the queue is durable

> *Does a queued prompt survive navigation and reload? The in-flight stream
> does. If the queue does not, the two halves of one turn behave differently
> and a follow-up vanishes silently. Matching it costs a migration.*

**Decision: durable, server-side, and 5.3 pays the migration.**

The PRD's symmetry argument is real but it is the weakest of the three, and it
is weaker than it looks: the stream survives a reload precisely *because it
was never client state*. `loadConversation` spots a trailing `generating` reply
and re-tails it, and the server replays `stream_buffer` from offset 0. Matching
that with browser storage would match it in one browser profile, which is not
the same shape of durability at all.

The two arguments that actually decide it:

**1.1 A client-only queue has no authority to arbitrate against a server that
already ends pauses unilaterally.** `close_orphaned_pause`
(`api/app/chats/views.py:43-100`) ends every `awaiting_input` reply in a chat
the moment any user message is posted — called from **both** write paths,
`StreamRepliesView.create` (`views.py:355`) and `MessageView.perform_create`
(`views.py:445`). So "do not let a queue START a turn into a pause" is a
data-integrity rule, not a courtesy. A rule whose only enforcement lives in a
tab that can be closed, duplicated or reloaded is a rule that will be broken,
and there is nowhere in a browser to put the refusal that a second tab would
have to respect.

**1.2 And the corollary that constrains 5.3 hardest: the server must not run
the queue itself.** This is not preference. `messages/latest/` is literally the
newest row in the chat by `created_at` (`api/app/chats/views.py:407-411`), and
`finishStream` reconciles a finished reply against it behind
`if (latest && latest.is_agent_response)`. If the server writes a queued *user*
row when a turn settles, that branch is false: the reply keeps its client-side
id `"streaming"`, never gets its `model_usage` (so feedback has nothing to
attach to), and `mergeServerActivity` never runs — so the server's
authoritative answered-question receipt never lands. **Every `ai.js` ever
shipped does this**, which makes a server-side drainer a fleet-wide regression
that no CDN push can outrun.

The queue is therefore **durable state that only a live client fires**. Said
plainly, because it is the cost of the decision: close the laptop mid-turn and
your follow-ups are still there when you come back — as a list, with a button.
They do not run while you are away. That is deliberate twice over: a turn
nobody is watching can ask a question nobody will read, and can spend money
with nobody able to stop it.

### 1.3 What the loser gives up, in both directions

**Client-only (localStorage / sessionStorage) is cheap and loses:**

* **the second tab, entirely.** `ai.js` has no `BroadcastChannel` and no
  `storage` listener. Two tabs on one chat means two independent queues, each
  firing on its own view of `S.sending`, into a server with no guard against a
  second reply while one is `generating`. Two concurrent replies then reconcile
  against the same `messages/latest/` and merge each other's content.
* **any authoritative order.** "See, reorder and delete" needs something to
  reorder *against*. Two tabs showing two different orders for one chat are
  both correct locally and there is no arbiter.
* **incognito.** `sessionStorage` is persisted for session restore by real
  browsers. Writing a queued prompt for a chat the API deliberately purges
  (`Chat.purge_stale_incognito`) puts those words on disk on a shared machine.
  That is a privacy regression, not a UX one.

**Server-durable costs 5.3** a model, a migration, four endpoints, and a queue
that can now answer `409`. That last part is the point: it is where the
invariant in §4 gets *enforced* rather than hoped for.

---

## 2. The model

```jsonc
QueuedPrompt = {
  "id":         "<uuid>",          // stable for the item's whole life
  "chat":       "<chat uuid>",     // FK — see §2.1, this is load-bearing
  "position":   1,                 // orderable; see §3
  "content":    "then convert it to EUR",   // the person's words, verbatim
  "state":      "queued",          // queued | held | claimed
  "client_id":  "…",               // client-supplied; makes POST idempotent
  "created_at": "2026-08-15T10:00:00Z"
}
```

Owner-scoped exactly the way `AnswerView` is. `content` is the person's own
text and is bounded and control-character-stripped on the way in, like every
other stored string on this surface.

### 2.1 Queue rows hang off `Chat`. Never off `Message`.

This is the most important line in the document and it is checkable today.
`pending_turn={}` is written by at least six paths already in `main`:

* `views.py:95` — `close_orphaned_pause`
* `approvals.py:304` — decline
* `prompts.py:3204` — quota refusal on resume
* `prompts.py:3321` — resume settle
* `prompts.py:3337` — resume failure
* and the first-hop settle

`close_orphaned_pause` clears `stream_buffer` in the same `UPDATE`. A queue
parented to the `Message` — whether as a relation or as a key inside
`pending_turn` — is destroyed by every one of those writes, and 5.5's abort
will add a seventh. **That is opencode's #5333 reproduced by code that is
already deployed, before anything called "interrupt" exists.** Keying the
queue to the chat is what makes "survives an interrupt" structural rather than
a promise somebody has to remember.

### 2.2 `client_id`, and why it is not the same as an idempotency key

`POST` is the one queue write whose lost response is genuinely ambiguous: the
client cannot tell "not queued" from "queued, response lost", and retrying
blind adds the prompt twice. A client-supplied `client_id`, unique per chat,
makes the retry a no-op that returns the existing row.

This does **not** contradict §3 of the question contract ("retry is always safe
and needs no idempotency key"). That statement is about a *claim*, which is a
conditional `UPDATE` and therefore self-refusing. An insert is not, and this is
the difference.

---

## 3. Order, and reordering

**`position` is the order and nothing else is.** The client sorts by
`position` ascending and never by `created_at` — a reordered queue is
deliberately not in the order it was typed, and the two must not be able to
disagree. This mirrors §7's rule for question options: order is the rank, and
the UI must not sort by anything else.

**Reorder is one write, and it is conditional.** `PATCH …/queue/<id>/` with a
target position rewrites the affected span server-side and returns the whole
list in its new order. It is expressed as a conditional write — the same shape
`questions.claim` and `approvals.claim` already use — for the reason those
state: two tabs reordering the same list with a read-then-write is a lost
update, and the loser must be told rather than silently overwritten.

**The client does not send positions it computed.** It sends "put item X at
index N" and takes the server's answer as the truth, so a reorder racing an
enqueue cannot produce two rows claiming position 3.

### 3.1 Delete

`DELETE …/queue/<id>/`, idempotent — deleting an item another tab already
removed is a success, not a `404` the person has to interpret.

### 3.2 What the client does with the order

Reordering is by **buttons, not drag**, and that is a UI decision the contract
records because it constrains nothing on the server and would otherwise be
re-litigated. A two-or-three-row strip that repaints under a streaming reply,
on touch, with no keyboard story, is the mechanism most likely to *lose* an
item on a mis-drop — and losing an item is the entire failure this feature
exists to prevent. Drag may be added later; it must never be the only path.

Arrows move focus and never reorder (§7's rule for the question card, for the
same reason). `Alt+Arrow` reorders the focused row. Bare `Delete`/`Backspace`
is deliberately unbound: a destructive default with no undo, on a strip a
keyboard user lands in by arrowing.

### 3.3 The approval pause renders. It is not a gap the contract works around.

An earlier draft of this document recorded, as an accepted cost, that **an
approval pause does not render on the live turn at all** — and then leaned on
that gap to justify a client-side lock standing in for the missing card. Both
halves were wrong, and the second one shipped a permanent freeze (§6.1).

The rendering defect was one missing sync site. `approvalPromptNode` was
reached only from `renderAiMessage`, which builds a reply node **once**;
`paintStream` thereafter rewrote the bubble, the meta and the questions on
every frame and never re-read `pendingToolStep`. `ai.js` now has
`syncApproval(node)` beside `syncQuestions(node)` at every site, and the
approval container is appended to every reply for the same reason the question
box is: an approval that arrives *after* the node was built needs somewhere to
land. The strip's copy is no longer imprecise, because the pause is visible.

**Still recommended for 5.3, and still not required: publish `Message.state`
verbatim** as an additive, read-only field beside `generating` — never
replacing it, because every shipped `ai.js` reads `generating` off the wire.
`MessageSerializer` (`api/app/chats/serializers.py:119-132`) publishes only the
derived `generating`, which deliberately collapses `generating` and
`awaiting_input`. Nothing in 5.4 depends on it: the client infers a pause from
the **trail** (§4.2), which is strictly better than inferring it from
`generating` and is what makes the gate survive a 500. `state` would let the
strip distinguish "working" from "waiting on you" in its own sentence, which is
polish, not safety.

---

## 4. The pending question — the collision, and the two guarantees

**Nothing may be enqueued, and nothing may run BY ITSELF, while any reply in
the chat is `awaiting_input`.**

**And a person may always act.** These are not in tension, and reading them as
if they were is what produced the state 5.4 shipped into review: a queue with
no button, a composer that swallowed every message, and no control anywhere to
end the pause. §4.4 states the second rule properly.

### 4.1 Why refusing an automatic run is not politeness

A queued prompt that runs posts a user message, and `close_orphaned_pause`
(`views.py:43-100`) ends the pause *on exactly that event*: the question is
stamped `expired`, `pending_turn` and `stream_buffer` are cleared, the trail is
stamped settled and open approvals are abandoned. The card the person is
looking at becomes *"This question wasn't answered."* while their answer is
still half-typed beneath it.

So an item that *could* be queued during a pause needs only one race, one
second tab, or one future abort path to destroy the pause. An item that cannot
exist needs none.

### 4.2 The guard that matters is at run time — and it is read off the TRAIL

A question can arrive **after** an item was queued — queued during ordinary
streaming, and then the reply asks. No add-time check can reach that case, and
it is the one that silently destroys a pause. **If one line of this contract
survives, make it this one.**

The first cut of the client half satisfied it *parasitically*: the gate read
`generating` off `messages/latest/`, a single GET. Driven, with only that route
varied and the question card still on the screen in all three:

| `messages/latest/` answers | queued prompt |
| --- | --- |
| `{generating: true}` | held — the guard works |
| `500` | **posted straight through the open question** |
| `{}` (every server too old to know the field) | **posted straight through the open question** |

Server-side that second POST runs `close_orphaned_pause`: the question stamped
`expired`, the turn behind it reclaimed, `abandon_open_actions` called. Reached
automatically, by a queue, with nobody having pressed anything.

So the client's gate is now **`pendingHumanStep(trailingReply())`** — a
question step still `pending`, or a tool step still `pending`. The trail
arrives on the socket this client is already reading and on every `messages/`
list; it is there when the reconcile is not. The wire field is still consulted
(`msg.generating === true`) but only as an *additional* reason to hold, never
as the only one. `commitStream` follows the same rule in the other direction:
it stamps a reply finished only when the reconcile actually returned that
reply, so a 500 or an old server's `{}` no longer settles a pause the server is
still holding.

Therefore, binding on 5.3:

* `POST …/queue/` returns **`409 awaiting_input`** while any reply in the chat
  is `AWAITING_INPUT`, echoing the authoritative question the way `AnswerView`
  already does.
* `POST …/queue/<id>/claim/` returns **`409 question_pending`** under the same
  condition — and the claim re-checks it *inside* the conditional `UPDATE`,
  not before it. A check-then-act here is a race whose loser expires somebody's
  question.
* The client re-checks every gate immediately before it fires (`drainQueue` in
  `ai.js`), and holds visibly when any gate fails. **This is a courtesy. The
  server is the mechanism** — the same sentence §3 of the question contract
  already uses about double answers, and for the same reason: a second tab or
  a stale build can always try.

### 4.3 What typing means while a question is pending

**It is refused, not queued, and the words stay in the box.**

Routing composer text to the answer endpoint was already rejected in §4.5: the
composer is the conversation channel, and an answer is a tool result bound to a
specific `question_id`, so *"actually stop, forget it"* would be recorded as
the answer to *"which account?"*. **Queueing reaches the same harm by a longer
road** — somebody typing at a question card is most likely typing an answer,
and the queue would take those words and send them later as a new turn.

So the shipped 5.2 behaviour is kept exactly: a real `disabled`, the
placeholder *"Answer above to carry on"*, and a blocked Enter that scrolls to
the card and pulses it.

Two things had to be added before *"the words stay in the box"* was true rather
than merely intended:

* they survive the next re-render (§6.3), or the promise expires at the first
  token-less commit;
* **the queue's own row control cannot take them.** `unqueueToComposer` was
  `input.innerText = item.text` — a replace. Driven with a question card on
  screen and a half-typed answer in the box, one click on a queued row deleted
  the answer and left no trace of it anywhere. The queue reaching an answer at
  *click* is the same harm as reaching it at *Enter*, arrived at from the
  opposite side. It is refused during a pause, and everywhere else it is a
  **swap**: the words in the box take the row's place, in that position, and
  one more click puts everything back.

### 4.4 A person's press is never refused for a reason they cannot see or undo

The rule §4.1 states is about what the software does **on its own**. Extending
it to what a *person* may do produced, driven, a chat that could never be sent
in again for the life of the page:

* `queueBusy()` folded "a reply the server says is generating" into the
  composer's lock. That fact has no release path — `finishStream` writes
  `generating: true` once and nothing re-reads it — so an approval pause or a
  fifteen-minute tail limit, both *designed* server behaviour, latched it on
  forever.
* `runnable` excluded the `running` state, which is exactly the state the latch
  produced. So there was no *Send next* either.
* The note read *"Sending when this reply finishes"* about a reply that had
  already committed, indefinitely, and the send button was `disabled: false`
  while doing nothing.
* Pulling a row back into the box and pressing Enter simply re-queued it.

Every message typed went into a list that could never fire. **This was a
regression for somebody who never wanted a queue**: before 5.4 the same state
let Enter through, and shipped 5.1 defines that a new user message is precisely
what ends a pause. A safety rule a person cannot get out of is not a safety
rule; it is the freeze this whole PRD exists to remove, relocated.

So the client half draws the line at **who acted**:

| | automatic drain | Enter in the box | *Send next* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| an answerable question card is on screen | refused | refused, points at the card | not offered |
| this client's own turn is in flight | waits for the commit | queues | not offered |
| the trailing reply is unsettled and no socket of ours will end it | **refused** | **sends** | **offered** |
| nothing outstanding | drains one | sends | offered |

Row three is the correction. The queue still never *starts* one of those turns
— that is §4.1, intact — but the person has the box, the button, and the
approval card's own Allow/Decline, and the strip says *"Paused — the last reply
didn't finish"* instead of promising a send.

### 4.5 §4.5's other open question is closed — by 5.1, not by this document

§4.5 left open *"what a new user message does to a chat whose last reply is
`awaiting_input`"*. **5.1 decided it and shipped it.** `close_orphaned_pause`'s
own docstring says so in terms: the decision is that a new user message *ends*
the pause. The queue contract records the answer and does not re-open it — and
§4.4 above is what it costs to be consistent with it: a client that made that
message impossible to send was disagreeing with its own server, silently.

What it forces on the queue is stated in §4.1: the queue's job is to never be
the thing that triggers it *on its own*. If an **automatic** run ever closes a
pause, that is a contract violation and should be counted as one, not logged as
a normal outcome — note that `close_orphaned_pause` iterates a *list*
(`views.py:89-91`), because two replies in one chat can be paused at once.

## 5. Interrupt — written before 5.5 existed

This section was written before 5.5 (reliable abort) existed, so that 5.5
could not settle it by accident in whatever file happened to kill the worker
— which at the time was a file that writes `pending_turn={}`. **5.5 has since
landed and is bound by every word of it; §5.2 records what it did.**

**Five invariants, binding on 5.5:**

1. **An interrupt never discards the queue.** That is #5333 verbatim: a queue
   that lived inside the running fiber, so interrupting the turn silently
   discarded everything behind it.
2. **An interrupt never runs the queue.** Every queued prompt was written for
   a world in which the aborted turn succeeded. Running one is the inverse
   failure and is worse, because it *acts*: you pressed stop and it started the
   next thing.
3. **An interrupt moves the queue to `held`, durably, and writes that
   BEFORE the worker is signalled.** Order matters: "the turn ended" is the
   run trigger, so killing first leaves a settle that is indistinguishable
   from a clean completion to anything watching. This is the same discipline
   as writing the answer into the trail inside the claim statement.
4. **An interrupt never silently deletes.** If a later product decision wants
   abort-clears-queue, it is an explicit, visible, undoable act with its own
   control — never a side effect of stop.
5. **Every turn-ending path must state its queue effect**, and the
   enumeration has to be COMPLETE — a path nobody listed is a path nobody
   fenced, which is how two of the entries below came to be wrong in the
   review of 5.5 rather than in the design of it. There are eight:

   | path | queue effect |
   | --- | --- |
   | normal settle (`prompts.run_generation`'s finalize) | **drains one**, and it is the only path that ever does |
   | worker failure (the `except` arm, and the `error` event that reaches a watching client) | **holds** |
   | quota refusal on resume | **holds** |
   | `approvals.decline` | **holds**, durably, and when it is a *Decline* it marks the reply stopped as well — see §5.3 |
   | `close_orphaned_pause` | **nothing**: it runs *inside* the send that ends the pause, so the queue is already being carried on by the act that reached it. A pause somebody had asked to stop is settled as a stop instead |
   | the reconciler's sweep | **holds** (no client is watching; the next one to look finds a held queue) |
   | **the stop** (5.5) | **holds**: `chats/stop.py`'s `hold_queue` moves every `queued` row in the chat to `held`, chat-scoped, in one statement, before the intent is written and before the worker can possibly notice. `claimed` rows are left alone |
   | **the tail's idle settle** (`prompts.tail_message`) | **holds** when a stop was already requested, by settling it as one; otherwise it is an ordinary incomplete turn and holds through `turnUnsettled` |

   Nothing is ever drained by an interrupt and nothing is ever deleted by
   anything. **`AWAITING_INPUT_TAIL_LIMIT` is explicitly NOT a turn-ending
   path** — it reclaims a socket, not a turn, exactly as §4.2 of the question
   contract says. A queue design that does not enumerate these *is* #5333.

   The two that were wrong, both found by driving the table rather than
   reading it:

   * **worker failure said "holds" and drained.** A worker that dies
     server-side rejects nobody's read: it writes an `error` event into the
     buffer, settles the reply FAILED and closes the socket **cleanly**, so
     it arrived at `commitStream` down the finished-turn path. `handleEvent`
     set `aiMsg.error` and nothing downstream read it. §6.2 already had the
     rule — *a prompt sent on top of an error hides the error* — and named
     only `failStream` and the two send catches, which is the exit this
     failure does not take. `commitStream` now reads `st.stopped ||
     aiMsg.stopped || aiMsg.error`;
   * **the tail's idle settle was not on the list at all.** It buried a
     presumed-dead producer with a bare `update(state=DONE)` — no
     `stop_requested_at` term and no `stopped_at` — so a reply somebody had
     already asked to stop ended as an ordinary completion, with no death
     certificate and no mark on the wire, and every observer that had not
     pressed the button drained. It is reachable exactly when somebody is
     most likely to press: a worker blocked past `IDLE_TIMEOUT`.

### 5.1 The client half, and why invariant 2 needed a mechanism rather than a claim

An earlier draft asserted that "`ai.js` already implements the client half of
this rule and it is tested". Half true, and the tested half was the easy one.

There are exactly two exits from `pumpFrames`:

* a **rejected** `read()` → `failStream` → `holdQueue`. Correct, and it is the
  shape the only interrupt test used (`droppingReader`).
* a resolved **`{done: true}`** → `finishStream` → `commitStream` →
  `drainQueue`. And *that* is what a stop produces: `reader.cancel()`, or the
  server closing the SSE when a stop kills the worker, is byte-for-byte a
  completed turn.

Driven, one queued follow-up in each:

| abort shape | posts | queue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| rejected read | `["pay the invoice"]` | held |
| **clean close** | `["pay the invoice", "then convert it to EUR"]` | **empty — it fired** |

Nothing observable distinguishes them, so the client cannot infer it. It has to
be **told**, and there was no state on the stream to tell it with — which meant
5.5 could not have satisfied invariant 2 even if it wanted to.

`ai.js` now has `stopStream(st, why)`: it marks the stream, cancels our reader,
and `commitStream` holds the queue instead of draining it whenever the mark is
present. **5.5 must call it before it signals the worker**, which is the client
mirror of invariant 3.

It is not dead code waiting for 5.5. This surface already has one interrupt —
**Decline** on an approval cancels the whole cascade — and it now goes through
`stopStream`. There is a test, and a mutation twin that removes the mark and
watches the refused plan get carried straight on with.

### 5.2 What 5.5 actually did, and the one thing §5.1 could not have known

`stopReply` calls `stopStream` and `holdQueue` **before** the POST, which is
invariant 3's client mirror. The composer is held shut for the length of the
request by `S.stopping[chatId]` rather than by the stream, because
`commitStream` frees `S.sending` the instant our reader is cancelled — which
is *before* the server has confirmed anything, and pressing Regenerate in that
window started a second worker on a reply that may still have been alive.

**The mark on the stream is not enough, and that is the correction §5.1 could
not make from inside one tab.** `stopStream` marks the stream of the tab that
pressed. Every other observer — a second tab, or this one after a reload
re-tailed the turn — sees a clean socket close and nothing else, and drains.
So the server says it out loud: the worker emits
`__WP_EVENT__ {"type":"stopped"}` in the same statement as its settle (it has
to be the same statement — the producer owns `stream_buffer`, and by then the
flush is fenced), the tail replays it for a late reconnect, and `commitStream`
reads `st.stopped || aiMsg.stopped`. Both halves have mutation twins.

Two other things 5.5 added that this contract depends on:

* **the tail names the reply**, `__WP_EVENT__ {"type":"reply","id":…}`, once,
  before anything else. A live reply's client-side id is the literal string
  `"streaming"` until the reconcile, so there was nothing for a stop — or, it
  turns out, for the approval card's own POST — to address;
* **`stopped_at` on the wire**, additive beside `state`. A stopped reply *is*
  `done`, so every shipped ai.js renders it correctly as an ordinary settled
  turn with partial text; only a client that knows the field says *"you
  stopped this reply."* There is deliberately no fifth `Message.State`:
  `generating` derives from `LIVE_STATES`, so a new state reads as idle to
  every ai.js on the CDN while `close_orphaned_pause`, `ai_reconcile`, the
  tail's idle settle and `prompt_queue.claim` all skip it — the same failure
  `prompt_queue.claim`'s own docstring already drove one control to the left.

**And the sentence the strip says.** `queueNote` has a fourth state,
*"Stopped — nothing else was sent"*, because *"Paused — the last reply didn't
finish"* reads as an unexplained failure about something a person did on
purpose. The reason rides inside `S.queueHeld[chatId]`, which every other
reader tests only for truthiness, so it cost no guard.

**`stopReply`'s own hold is not redundant, and the test named for it did not
prove that.** Every assertion in *"the press marks the stream and holds the
queue BEFORE it signals"* was satisfied by two other mechanisms —
`S.stopping[chatId]` for the in-flight note, `commitStream`'s own hold for
the settled one — so deleting the call changed nothing the suite could see.
It is load-bearing on the path §5.2 exists for: `stopTarget()` also returns
the trailing unsettled reply when there is **no live stream** (the
fifteen-minute tail limit, or a reload onto a pause), and there
`commitStream` never runs at all. Without the press's own hold the strip
says *"Paused — the last reply didn't finish"* about a deliberate stop.
Driven, with a mutation twin.

### 5.3 A `202` is not an answer, and Decline is an interrupt

Two corrections that fall out of the same reading — *what does the client do
when it has been told the work is NOT dead?*

**`202 stopping` means the work is not dead**, so releasing on it is the
client-side half of the flip the PRD forbids. It used to: the lock came off
on any response, `queueState` fell through to `"stopped"`, which counts as
runnable, and the strip offered *Send next* on a reply the server had just
said it was still killing. One press then started a second worker into it,
and `prompt_queue.claim` deliberately refuses to widen to `LIVE_STATES`, so
there is no server-side backstop — the chat simply ends up with two
`generating` replies.

The endpoint is idempotent by construction and answers `200` the moment the
work IS dead, so **the request is its own confirmation**: the client asks
again on an interval until the answer changes, bounded past a container
command's own twenty-second timeout, and then says the half it cannot
promise. Keeping the mark up meanwhile is not the freeze this PRD exists to
remove — it is the state an ordinary in-flight reply already puts the
composer in, where typing queues.

**Decline is bound by all five invariants and was getting neither half of
what 5.5 built.** §5.1 names it as the interrupt this surface already had.
It wrote no `stopped_at`, so no death certificate and no `stopped` frame for
the tail to replay — every tab that did not press it saw a clean settle and
drained — and nothing held the durable queue, so invariant 3's *"durably"*
existed only in the pressing tab's memory. The asymmetry was the whole
argument: pressing **Stop** on a paused turn went through
`stop.settle_paused`, which writes the mark, the hold and the ledger's own
sentence; pressing **Decline** on the same pause wrote none of the three.
`approvals.decline(message, stopped=True)` now does all three. A failed
*resume* reaches the same function and takes the hold without the mark:
invariant 1 has no exception, but *"you stopped this reply"* is false about a
resume that could not start.

---

## 6. What `ai.js` does, that 5.3 can rely on

### 6.1 Three facts, and which reader is entitled to which

```text
waitingOnYou()    ⟺  pendingQuestionMsg() != null      // §4.1, unchanged
turnInFlight()    ⟺  S.sending || an open stream in this realm
turnUnsettled(c)  ⟺  the TRAILING reply in c has a pending question or tool
                     step, or the server said generating: true for it
```

* the **composer** reads the first two, and only those;
* the **queue's automatic drain** reads all three;
* the **queue's press** reads the first two.

This replaces a single `queueBusy()` that all three shared, and the change is
not a refactor. `queueBusy` folded the server's `generating` into the
composer's lock, and §4.4 is the driven account of what that cost. Two
narrower defects fell out of the same fold and are fixed here:

* **`generating` is a one-way latch.** `finishStream` only ever sets it true;
  `commitStream` only ever sets it false when it is not already true; nothing
  re-reads `latest` for that message afterwards. Anything using it as a lock
  needs a release path, and there is none. It is now advisory, and only for the
  queue.
* **It was scanned across every message in the thread.** A stale mid-thread
  `generating: true` row is ordinary output from today's API —
  `StreamRepliesView.create` writes the row `state=GENERATING` before the
  worker runs, nothing clears it but tailing that exact message, and
  `close_orphaned_pause` filters `AWAITING_INPUT` only. `close_orphaned_pause`'s
  own docstring names the state: *two replies in one chat both serialise
  `generating: true`*. One such row wedged the chat through reloads and
  navigations, because `loadConversation` re-tails only the **trailing**
  generating reply and that one never is. Only the trailing reply is read now,
  for exactly that reason.

The genuine §6.1 fix from the first cut stands, and it is the one that belongs
to the *question*, not to `generating`:

> After the fifteen-minute tail limit drops the socket on a still-paused turn,
> `commitStream` frees `S.sending` while `pendingQuestionMsg()` still finds
> the question. The send button was correctly `disabled`; `submitFromInput`
> guarded on `S.sending` alone, so **Enter posted a second turn and started a
> second reply stream** — which server-side runs `close_orphaned_pause` and
> destroys the agent's half-built turn.

`submitFromInput` reads `waitingOnYou()`. That lock is safe to hold precisely
because **the card is its release**: answer it and it lifts. A lock whose
release is a field nobody re-reads is a freeze.

**The rule the send button follows: it is `disabled` exactly when pressing it
would do nothing.** True of a pause with an answer card. False of an ordinary
in-flight reply, which queues. False of a stalled turn, which sends.

### 6.2 Only the chat on screen runs, and only off a commit this client watched

This is mechanical, not a judgement call. `postAndStream` reads `S.chatId` and
appends to the module-level `messagesEl`, so running an off-screen chat's queue
would push its user message into the *visible* chat's pane. And `S.stream` is a
single slot, so a chat cannot start a turn while another chat is streaming.

Consequences, stated plainly:

* A queue in a chat you are not looking at does not run. It stays visible, and
  never looks sent, so it is there when you return — which is why the
  visibility requirements are load-bearing and not decoration.
* Auto-running happens **only** in `commitStream`, after the reconcile and the
  fold, and only when the turn both ENDED and ended WELL — no stop mark from
  either source (§5.1, §5.2) and no error on the reply. Not `failStream`, not
  either send catch: a prompt sent on top of an error hides the error. That
  last clause used to name only the two paths that reject a read, and a
  server-side death takes neither of them — see invariant 5's table.
* Exactly **one** item runs per commit, never a loop, so every prompt gets a
  turn boundary at which a person can intervene.

### 6.3 The draft, which is half the problem and has nothing to do with the queue

Driven: a reply that streams no tokens commits through `renderConversation`,
which rebuilds the composer — and the in-progress text goes with it, with
nothing on screen to say it ever existed. That is where the work is actually
lost today, not at Enter.

`ai.js` carries the composer's text across a rebuild, keyed by chat, in memory.
It is keyed to the chat the *old* composer belonged to, so a draft never
follows you into a different conversation, and it is never written to storage,
so an incognito chat's draft cannot outlive its tab.

### 6.4 A send that never reached the server

`drainQueue` takes the head **before** the send. Restoring it only on a
synchronous throw was wrong: `postAndStream` returns a promise, so the
realistic failure — offline, dropped connection — lands in its `.catch`, and
the item was destroyed there.

The justification offered for that was the optimistic echo already on the
thread. Driven, the echo is a phantom: `userMsg` keeps its `local-` id, the
server never received it, it is visually identical to a delivered message,
there is no failed marker and no retry, and one navigation away and back erases
it. So:

* the phantom is **removed from the thread**, because a message that was never
  delivered must not look delivered;
* the words go **back to the head of the queue**, held, with *Send next* on the
  strip.

This is now the only path on the surface where a failed send is recoverable at
all — an ordinary typed message whose POST fails takes it too, rather than
leaving a bubble the next refetch deletes and a sentence naming no message.

### 6.5 The landing

A chat that does not exist yet cannot hold a queue: there is nowhere to show
one, and running it would have to create the chat. So `/new` during a reply
elsewhere is **locked and says so** — *"Wait for the current reply to
finish"* — rather than queueing into a chat id about to be replaced. Before
this, that press was the quietest failure on the surface: it fired no request
and said nothing.

The landing's other quiet failure was a chat create that the server refused.
The box had already been emptied, and the error line went to a thread the
landing does not have, so the message was simply gone. A failed create now
puts the words back in the box and the files back as chips. It never
overwrites anything typed since. If the person has navigated away, the words
are kept as that landing's draft instead.

### 6.6 Queue for later: ⌘/Ctrl+Enter on an idle chat

The composer's hint reads *"↵ to send, ⌘↵ to queue for later"*. In a
conversation with no reply running, ⌘+Enter (Ctrl+Enter elsewhere; both are
accepted everywhere) adds the prompt to the strip in the **ready** state and
sends nothing. It leaves the queue the way any ready item does: after the next
reply this tab **watches land** (§6.2), or when somebody presses *Send next*.
No new automatic trigger is added. A ready item in an idle chat therefore waits
until the person sends something else or presses the button.

While a reply runs, Enter and ⌘+Enter both queue, as Enter always has. There
is no "send now" mid-reply: the server allows one live reply per chat
(`claim_reply_slot`, 409), and a stop-then-send would break §5's promise that
a stop sends nothing else. On the landing, ⌘+Enter simply sends, because there
is nothing to queue behind (§6.5). A slash command, an open question and an
upload still in flight are handled first, exactly as for Enter.

### 6.7 Offline

When the browser says it is offline (`navigator.onLine === false`, then the
window's `offline` and `online` events), Enter in a conversation **queues
instead of posting**. The strip shows the item as *Not sent yet* with *Send
next*. Its durable add fails like any other, so the row stays rowless and the
unload guard counts it. On the landing the words stay in the box.

Coming back online clears the notice and **sends nothing**. Only a watched
commit or a press sends, and being offline does not loosen that rule. The
offline flag is a hint and never a gate on a press: *Send next* and the drain
do not read it, so a browser that is wrong about being offline cannot trap a
message.

---

## 7. CDN independence — useful, with the bound on the screen

`ai.js` ships to `cdn.workpeg.com` on every green pipeline and runs against
servers of every age. Until 5.3 lands that is **every** server, including
production.

**The answer is: useful, not merely harmless — and it makes zero new
requests.** 5.4's queue is memory, per chat, for the life of the page.

An earlier draft said this and was **wrong about why**, in a way worth keeping
on the record because it is the trap: *"there is no capability probe, because
'asks for nothing' is a stronger CDN-independence property than any probe could
be."* Making no new requests does not make a feature independent of the server
when its only safety gate is a **field on an existing response**. Driven, that
gate failed on a 500 and failed on an old server's `{}` (§4.2), and the same
field wedged the composer shut against servers behaving exactly as designed
(§4.4). Two sections of this document then contradicted each other about
whether the queue depended on the server, and the driven behaviour matched the
one that admitted it did.

It is true now, and for a reason that is checkable rather than rhetorical:

* the composer's behaviour depends on **no server field at all** — only on this
  client's own `S.sending` and its own open socket;
* the queue's pause gate is the **trail**, which arrives on the socket this
  client is already reading and on every `messages/` list, and is therefore
  present on every server that can serve a conversation at all;
* `generating` is consulted only as an *additional* reason to hold, so a server
  that never sends it costs one press of *Send next* and nothing else;
* there is a test that drives a full mount → stream → queue → drain with
  `window.Workpeg` entirely absent, and one that drives the pause gate against
  `latest` answering `500` and `{}`.

**The bound, stated on the strip and not only here** — and since 7.6 it is
stated CONDITIONALLY, because for most chats it is no longer the truth (§10):
the queue is lost on a reload. The strip carries the line *"Kept in this tab until sent"*, in all
eight catalogues, and a reload or a tab close with anything queued fires a
`beforeunload` guard — armed only while there is something to lose, because a
page that argues about every unload is a page people learn to click through.
That is open question 12's stated harm — *"a follow-up vanishes silently"* —
answered in the only place it can be answered before 5.3 lands: out loud,
before it costs somebody something.

Deliberately **not** done in the interim: a `localStorage`/`sessionStorage`
queue. It looks like the pragmatic middle and is the worst option available.
Its one honest case — reload in a single tab — is exactly the case a demo
exercises, so it would ship looking correct and fail on second tabs, on
incognito chats and on background streams, invisibly. And migrating a
half-trusted local queue into a server model later is strictly harder than
starting with the model.

Two further constraints this build satisfies, from §6.2 of the question
contract, both of which were live traps:

* **No new icon name.** `_runtime_base_icons()` in `build.py` scrapes icon
  names out of the *bundled* runtime JS at build time and `icons.css` is subset
  to them, so a name only the new `ai.js` mentions is a blank square in every
  app built before this ships — invisible from in here, because a fresh build
  always contains it. The strip uses `arrow-up`, `arrow-down` and `x`, each
  already named by a pre-5.4 bundle for another reason. `chevron-up`,
  `pencil` and `player-play` are in none of them and were rejected on that
  basis alone. There is a test.
* **Every container is inert when empty.** The queue strip and the new approval
  container are both appended to every conversation, including on servers that
  will never have a queue, so both are genuinely childless and hidden by
  `:empty{display:none}` — "renders nothing" is not "occupies nothing".

Nothing in the queue calls `Workpeg.renderNode` or `renderJSON`, and it touches
no `Workpeg.*` helper at all.

---

## 8. The endpoints 5.3 must add

```text
GET    /v1/businesses/<business>/chats/<chat>/queue/
POST   /v1/businesses/<business>/chats/<chat>/queue/
PATCH  /v1/businesses/<business>/chats/<chat>/queue/<id>/     # position
DELETE /v1/businesses/<business>/chats/<chat>/queue/<id>/
POST   /v1/businesses/<business>/chats/<chat>/queue/<id>/claim/
```

Auth is the shape `answers/` and `approvals/` accept: `credentials: "include"`,
`Content-Type: application/json`, **no CSRF header** — `ai.js` has none to send
and this cannot be fixed from `ai.js` if it diverges.

| Status | When |
| --- | --- |
| `409 awaiting_input` | enqueue while a reply in this chat is paused (§4.2) |
| `409 question_pending` | claim while a reply in this chat is paused (§4.2) |
| `409 already_claimed` | another tab claimed this item first |
| `409 stale_position` | the conditional reorder lost (§3) |
| `400 empty_content` | nothing to queue |

`code` is stable and machine-readable and is never localised; `detail` is the
human sentence and may be translated. `409` and `400` mean opposite things to
the client — settle and stop offering, versus re-enable and let them retry —
which is the distinction §3 of the question contract had to add and which
should not have to be added twice.

### 8.1 What must be atomic

1. **The claim.** A single conditional `UPDATE` from `queued` to `claimed`,
   with the `awaiting_input` check *inside* the same statement. A second tab
   loses the race and is refused rather than firing the same prompt twice.
   Reuse the shape `questions.claim` and `approvals.claim` already have; do not
   invent a second one.
2. **The reorder.** One statement or one transaction over the affected span,
   conditional on the positions the client last saw. Read-then-write loses an
   update whenever two tabs reorder together.
3. **The enqueue.** Unique on `(chat, client_id)`, so a retry after a lost
   response returns the existing row instead of adding a second (§2.2).

### 8.2 What the client will do with a refusal

A `409 question_pending` on a claim is a **hold, not an error**: the strip shows
*"Waiting on your answer above"* and offers no run, exactly as it does when its
own gate fires. It is never surfaced as a failed send, because nothing failed
and nothing was lost.

A claim that succeeds and whose subsequent message POST fails must return the
item to `queued` at its original position (§6.4's rule, server-side). A claimed
row with no turn behind it is the durable version of the phantom bubble.

### 8.3 What must NOT be built

**A worker that runs the queue.** It is the obvious improvement and it is
wrong three times over: it breaks `messages/latest/` for every `ai.js` on the
CDN (§1.2), it lets a closed tab spend money with nobody able to abort it, and
it can walk into a question nobody is there to read. The queue is durable
*state*; a live client is the only thing that starts a turn. Write it down,
because somebody will suggest it.

**A server-side lock on the composer.** Whatever 5.3 adds, it must not give the
client a reason to refuse a person's own message that the person cannot see and
cannot clear. §4.4 is the driven cost of exactly that, and it was reached from
a field that already existed.

---

## 9. Open questions for whoever implements 5.3

1. **Endpoint scoping.** `AnswerView` filters chat + owner but not
   `business_uuid`, identical to `ApprovalView` — so a queue endpoint inherits
   the same unresolved question §8.4 of the question contract already flags:
   whether `IsBusinessStaff` binds the URL's business to the staff row. Do not
   assume it is settled.
2. **`Message.state` on the wire** (§3.3). Additive and read-only. No longer
   load-bearing — the client infers a pause from the trail — but it is what
   would let the strip say "waiting on you" instead of "hasn't finished".
3. **The interleaving of a claim and an answer POST into the same chat.**
   `close_orphaned_pause` is a conditional `UPDATE` and cannot race the answer
   claim, so a clean `409` is expected — but the specific ordering is untested
   and should get a test in 5.3.
4. **Incognito.** `Chat.incognito` chats are purged lazily. A `QueuedPrompt`
   row for one must be purged with it, and should probably not be written at
   all.
5. **Reconciling the memory queue with the durable one, once.** When 5.3 lands,
   a page that already holds an in-memory queue will meet a server queue for
   the same chat. The rule should be decided in 5.3 and not improvised in the
   client: the server's list is the truth, and anything only the tab knows
   about is enqueued into it rather than dropped.
6. **Whether a `held` queue is durable state or a client-side view.** §5's
   invariant 3 says an interrupt writes `held` durably. The client currently
   derives its hold locally. If 5.3 stores it, the two need one owner, and the
   answer should be the server's.

---

## 10. What 7.6 built, and the one question it had to answer itself

5.3 shipped every endpoint in §8 and `ai.js` called none of them for weeks.
The list a person could see, reorder and delete was memory, and the strip said
so. 7.6 is the wire.

**The probe is one `GET`, and there is nothing else.** No flag, no version
field, no `OPTIONS`. That is not minimalism for its own sake — it is what
makes the awkward cases free. An incognito chat, a sub-agent's transcript, a
soft-deleted chat and a server that has never heard of a queue all answer the
identical `404`, so not one of them needs a branch, a vocabulary, or a
capability list that can go stale. The client has exactly two modes and the
GET decides which.

**A definite answer latches; an indefinite one must not.** `chat_for`'s
predicates cannot change while a page is open, so a `404` is a fact for the
life of that page. A dropped socket is not — and latching one would strand the
tab on a memory queue that a reload silently loses, which is §1's harm
reintroduced by the probe meant to remove it. 5xx and network failures are
therefore left unrecorded and asked again at the next thing that happens.

**The status alone is not evidence.** Durable mode needs 2xx *and* an actual
`queue` array. A captive portal, a proxy error page or a stubbed route
answering `200` with anything else would otherwise read as *"your queue is
empty"*, take the tab into durable mode against a server with no queue, and
make every add look like it landed. There is a test and a mutation twin.

**The head is not removed before the send.** §6.4 had to grow a restore path
for every way a send can fail precisely because memory mode keeps the prompt
inside a closure between the shift and the POST. A durable row is its own
escrow: it stays visible, in place, marked as sending, and the only thing that
removes it is the message insert actually landing — not the commit, because a
commit never runs for a chat you have navigated away from and a reload in
between would re-show a sentence that has already been said.

**The claim is the one verb that is never retried, and it is written apart
from `json()` to keep it that way.** A retry after a lost `202` answers
`409 already_claimed` and burns this tab's own grant for the length of the
server's grace, so the prompt sits there looking sent — by the mechanism meant
to stop it being sent twice. The shared helper's 401 re-issue happens to be
harmless (the view never runs, so no grant is minted), but the rule has to
hold by construction rather than as a property of a helper somebody may widen.

**Every gate is re-checked in the same tick between the `202` and the
insert.** §4.2 calls the client's re-check a courtesy. It is not one any more.
`claim`'s own docstring says the window cannot be closed server-side, and
§9.3's answer-first case is worse than that: answering a question moves the
reply out of `awaiting_input`, so the claim's guard finds nothing paused and
hands out a grant *into a resumed turn*. Widening the server's condition was
considered and refused for a good reason. This is the only thing standing
there.

**One new request, and it is spent at the drain.** No `BroadcastChannel`, no
`storage` listener, no polling, no `visibilitychange`. Correctness against a
second tab is carried by the server's refusals — the conditional claim, the
conditional reorder, the idempotent delete — so freshness only decides how
long the strip may show a stale picture, never whether a prompt is lost or
doubled. The exception is the automatic drain, which is the one place the
queue *acts* on the order it believes: nothing fences it claiming what this
tab thinks is the head after another tab reordered, because the claim succeeds
on any queued row. So a `GET` runs immediately before it, charged only to a
chat that has a durable queue with something in it, at a turn boundary
somebody is already waiting at.

**The window between a row appearing and the server having it**, which
adversarial review found and which is the subtlest thing here. `enqueue`
renders and POSTs, and the row is on the strip with no id for the length of
that round trip — during which the person can delete it, take it back into the
box, or the turn can end and drain it (a rowless head takes the memory path,
which sends it).

The add's own response then arrives and adopts the server's list, which
contains a row nothing local matches — so the prompt comes back. For a delete
that is a prompt somebody removed reappearing; for a drain it is worse, because
the sentence has already been *sent*, so it returns to the strip queued and the
next clean commit sends it again. Two user rows, two workers, two bills.

The fix is in the response handler, not the drain: if the item has left the
queue by the time its add lands, the row the server just made is **deleted**
rather than adopted. That covers all three exits with one rule. Holding the
drain until the add landed was tried and is worse — the commit is the only
moment the queue may run itself, so refusing there means the boundary passes
with the queue visibly not draining and the prompt waiting on a press nobody
knows is needed.

**A grant a dead tab left behind is handed back before it is taken.** The claim
accepts only `queued` or `held`, so a row still marked `claimed` refuses every
press for as long as it exists — and nothing in the API sweeps one, because
there is no lease and no reaper. Past the grace the server lets anybody return
it without a token, so the drain returns it first and then takes it properly.
Inside the grace the return is refused and the claim loses cleanly, which is
the honest answer: another tab really is sending it.

**A failed send is moved to the head after its add lands.** Everything this tab
holds is added at the TAIL, because a page that never saw the durable order
must not reshuffle it — but §6.4's rule is that a send that never reached the
server is the NEXT thing out, not the last. Both are satisfied by adding at the
tail and then moving it, once there is a row to move.

### 10.1 §9, closed

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **9.1** endpoint scoping | answered by 5.3 — `chat_for` filters `owner__business__uuid` explicitly as well as transitively |
| **9.2** `Message.state` on the wire | shipped, additive, still labelled polish; the gate is still the trail |
| **9.3** claim × answer interleaving | answered by test, and NOT the way this document expected — see the re-check above |
| **9.4** incognito | never written at all, and the whole surface `404`s, so the client needs no branch |
| **9.5** reconcile | decided in `prompt_queue.py`'s module docstring, in full. 7.6 implements it rather than improvising: one GET per (page, chat); the server's list is the truth for order and membership; every rowless local item is POSTed at the tail in local order; never the reverse merge; a reconcile refused by a pause is retried when the pause clears |
| **9.6** is `held` durable | **half answered, and the other half was 7.6's to decide.** The state is stored and the server owns it — but it does not *enforce* it: the claim accepts a held row on purpose, because a held row the claim refused would be a lock a person could see and not clear. So not auto-running a held item stays the client's rule |

**The half 9.6 left open** was the precedence between this tab's own hold and
the durable one. There is no `held_reason` column and `hold_queue` writes only
`state=HELD`, so the two carry different information and neither is a superset.

The answer is a **union, never last-writer-wins**. Held is a safety state, and
the safe merge of two independent *"do not run this automatically"* sources is
OR: nothing may make a held queue auto-runnable by accident. The local hold is
tested first so its *reason* still wins the sentence, and nothing an adopt
brings back ever clears it — a `queued` list is not evidence that a turn ended
well, because it cannot know about a rejected read, a failed insert, or a
reply that carried an error.

**What that costs, stated rather than hidden:** a tab that reloads onto rows
the server marked `held` can tell that the queue is held but not why, so it
says *"Paused — the last reply didn't finish"* even for a deliberate stop.
Inventing *"you stopped this reply"* would tell somebody they pressed a button
they never pressed. Recovering it means reading `Message.state`/`stopped_at`
off the trailing reply, which §9.2 shipped and labelled polish — worth doing,
not worth guessing.

### 10.2 The gap in §5's table, which is not the client's to close

Invariant 5 binds eight turn-ending paths and six say **holds**. `hold_queue`
is called from exactly two places in the whole API: the stop and the decline.
Worker failure, the quota refusal on resume, the reconciler's sweep and the
tail's idle settle write **no durable hold at all**.

7.6 compensates for one of them — `commitStream`'s `failed` branch mirrors the
hold from the client, which is why the durable push happens there and not in
`failStream` or the send catch (those are facts about *this tab's socket*, and
pausing every other tab's queue over one tab's bad connection is worse than
the failure it prevents). The other three are unreached by any client, because
no client is watching when they happen.

**This should be a server follow-up rather than more client compensation**, and
it is recorded here rather than fixed here because the table is the contract's
and the paths are the API's.
